slides.headline: Only about 50,000 Asian elephants are left in the wild.
slides.sub: Why the world's other elephant is in trouble

slides.headline: Endangered, and still decreasing
slides.body: IUCN has listed the Asian elephant as Endangered at every assessment since 1986, inferring a decline of at least 50% over three generations (~75 years).

slides.label: the range they once roamed, from West Asia to China
slides.body: Today: very roughly 486,800 km² in 13 countries, much of it fragmented. They are gone from West Asia, Java and most of China.

slides.label: elephants killed each year in conflict with people
slides.body: And more than 600 people. Conflict grows as farms, roads and railways cut into habitat; 80–85% of reported deaths are in India and Sri Lanka.

slides.headline: Over 60% live in one country
slides.body: India holds an estimated 29,964 of the 48,323–51,680 wild Asian elephants counted in 2018. Numbers have plummeted in Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Sumatra.

slides.headline: Where protection works, they recover
slides.body: Sri Lanka's population has increased, and much of southern India's Western Ghats population looks stable, likely thanks to conservation efforts.

slides.headline: Share this with someone who loves elephants.

caption:
Only about 50,000 Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) remain in the wild, and IUCN lists the species as Endangered.

The 2018 estimate of 48,323–51,680 is uncertain: elephants are hard to count in dense forest, and some national figures rest on interviews rather than surveys. The Sumatran subspecies is Critically Endangered. All photos were taken in Sri Lankan and Indian national parks; we left out photos of working and camp elephants.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: IUCN Red List, Elephas maximus (Williams et al. 2020, assessed 2019).
